# A pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model predicts tumor debulking improves CAR T-cell efficacy in Large B-Cell Lymphoma

**Authors:** Amy E. Pomeroy; Brian J. Sworder; Deborah Plana; Yanguang Cao; Ash A. Alizadeh; Adam C. Palmer

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Pharmacology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC | 2Computational Medicine Program, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC | 3UNC Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC | 4Division of Oncology, Department of Medicine, Stanford University, Stanford, CA | 5Laboratory of Systems Pharmacology and the Department of Systems Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 6Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 7Division of Pharmacotherapy and Experimental Therapeutics, Eshelman School of Pharmacy, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC | 8Stanford Cancer Institute, Institute for Stem Cell Biology & Regenerative Medicine, Stanford, CA

## Abstract

Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cells produce durable remissions in some large B-cell lymphoma patients, but outcomes are poor in patients with large tumor burdens or limited CAR T-cell expansion. To understand these relationships and explore potential interventions, we applied established population-pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic principles to model kinetics of axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) concentrations and tumor responses to axi-cel, and validated model outputs using independent cohorts. This mechanistic model reproduces and explains poor outcomes associated with high tumor burden and low CAR T-cell expansion, finding that proliferation of large lymphoma populations can outpace the cytotoxic effect of CAR T-cells. A high ratio of lymphoma cells to CAR T-cells is effectively a mechanism of CAR T-cell resistance, which could be modified by tumor debulking before infusion. This model predicts that reducing tumor burden before CAR T-cell infusion may improve durable remission rate. Future clinical studies optimizing bridging therapy may therefore enhance CAR T-cell therapies’ success.

## Introduction

Large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) is cured in many patients by combination chemoimmunotherapy. However, survival for patients with relapsed or refractory LBCL has historically been poor. Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies targeting CD19, a protein on the surface of B-cells, have demonstrated impressive efficacy in this setting. Three CD19-targeting CAR T-cell products have been approved for LBCL (1) including Axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel), which is approved for second-line treatment of primary refractory or fast relapsing LBCL based on the ZUMA-7 trial (2). Axi-cel achieved ≈40% rate of durable remission in this setting, which underscores the significant potential for improved approaches to benefit more patients. Multiple studies of CD19 CAR T-cell therapies for LBCL have identified initial tumor burden as a strong prognostic factor, and among tumor- and product-related features, the strongest predictor of outcome (3). This observation suggests the hypothesis that the efficacy of CAR T-cells could be improved by reducing tumor burden prior to CAR T-cell infusion.

Patients indicated for CAR T-cells generally have two windows of opportunity for lymphoma debulking by systemic and/or radiation therapy. First, ‘holding therapy’ may be applied between indication and leukapheresis (harvesting a patient’s T-cells), and second, ‘bridging therapy’ may be applied in the weeks between leukapheresis and CAR T-cell infusion. For the purpose of this study, we hereafter write ‘bridging’ to encompass both holding and bridging therapies, referring collectively to any tumor debulking treatment, whether radiation or systemic, administered between indication and infusion. These interventions have typically been reserved for patients with an urgent need for disease control due to rapidly progressing or bulky disease (1). Because bridging therapy is needed in high-risk patients, its use is associated with poor prognosis (4). This association with baseline risk may obscure the therapeutic effects of bridging and may have contributed to its reserved use. In the ZUMA-7 trial, which enrolled only patients who did not require intensive bridging therapy, the two-year event-free survival rate of 40% demonstrates that patients not identified as needing bridging therapy nevertheless need more effective treatment.

Many patients have unused opportunities for further tumor debulking, but its potential benefit is uncertain. Among patients who receive bridging, retrospective cohort studies have reported that tumor reduction from bridging is associated with improved efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy. Roddie et al. found that patients achieving a partial or complete response to bridging therapy had significantly reduced risk of progression and death (5), and Hubbeling et al. showed that patients whose tumor volume declined from high to low achieved outcomes comparable to those with initially low tumor volume (6). These observations support the hypothesis that debulking can improve the efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy, although they are non-randomized studies and do not investigate whether patients without bulky disease may also benefit from further reduction in tumor volume.

Here we investigate the effects of debulking therapies before CAR T-cell infusion using a mechanistic mathematical model calibrated on clinical trial outcomes. Given substantial patient-to-patient variability in CAR T-cell expansion and lymphoma response, we used a population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (pop-PK/PD) model of CAR T-cell therapy to explore possible clinical interventions. Pop-PK/PD models simulate patient cohorts wherein each individual’s parameters are sampled from distributions, so that cohorts reproduce relevant magnitudes of inter-patient variation in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Models of CAR T-cell PK/PD have contributed to the understanding and development of CAR T products (7). Across disease settings including leukemia, lymphoma, solid tumors, and mouse models, and diverse model methods, including differential equations (8–10), predator-prey models (11), stochastic simulations of tumor extinction (12), state transition models of memory/effector/exhausted phenotypes (13), and systems pharmacology models linking cytokines to CAR T-cell states (14), early CAR T-cell expansion and baseline tumor burden consistently emerge as dominant predictors of outcome. In particular, the ratio of CAR T-cell peak to number of tumor cells has been clinically validated as a strong predictor of durable response (15). Based on this insight, models have investigated means of enhancing CAR T-cell expansion and persistence - the numerator of this ratio - by approaches including personalized dosing or lymphodepletion (9,12,13), product engineering (13), cytokine support (14), and checkpoint blockade (8). We apply well-established pop-PK/PD principles to examine a complementary question: the potential of reducing the baseline number of cancer cells - the denominator of this ratio - to improve outcomes of CAR T-cell therapy. These approaches are not exclusive, and altering both numerator and denominator logically offers the greatest potential to improve response rate.

While models do not replace clinical study, like other preclinical methods, they can inform the development of clinical studies. In contrast to individual risk prediction models, which operate on statistical associations rather than mechanistic processes, pop-PK/PD models can simulate how different treatment approaches affect outcomes across populations. We calibrate this pop-PK/PD model on distributions of CAR T-cell kinetics and lymphoma responses to axi-cel therapy in human trials, validate the model on individual patient data from independent cohorts, and apply the model to investigate how tumor debulking prior to CAR T-cell infusion may change the rate of durable remission.

## Results

We built a pop-PK/PD model of axi-cel by combining a published pop-PK model (16) with a pharmacodynamic (PD) model of tumor killing by CAR T-cells. We calibrated the model to reproduce multiple clinical features of axi-cel kinetics and LBCL response. The pop-PK model of CD19 CAR T-cell therapy includes an initial CAR T expansion phase followed by a decline phase for two populations, effector T-cells and memory T-cells (16) (Figure 1A). The PD portion of the model describes established biology: lymphoma cells proliferate, and can be engaged and killed by CAR T-cells; no novel mechanisms are hypothesized (Figure 1A). Inter-patient heterogeneity is modeled as distributions of pharmacodynamic parameters, including clinically measured distributions of initial tumor burden and tumor cell proliferation rate (17), and a calibrated distribution of the rate of lymphoma cell killing by CAR T-cells. The published pop-PK model was calibrated on the pharmacokinetics of tisagenlecleucel, a CD19 CAR T-cell product, and here was re-calibrated (Table S1) to fit the pharmacokinetics of axi-cel measured in 162 patients (18) (Figure 1B, C). Pharmacodynamic parameters were fitted so the complete pop-PK/PD model reproduced the progression-free survival distribution (PFS) of axi-cel in second-line LBCL (Figure 1B, Table S2) (2). One expected difference between our model and clinical data is that in a simulation, disease progression can be rapidly identified in non-responding patients, whereas in clinical data, progression is observed at scheduled scan times (Figure 1B). Simulations of the pop-PK/PD model for a virtual patient cohort demonstrate how inter-patient differences in pharmacokinetics and initial tumor size lead to divergent pharmacodynamics of lymphoma cell death (Figure 1C). Together, these results recapitulate clinically observed kinetics and durations of tumor response after axi-cel.

Having calibrated the pop-PK/PD model on data from ZUMA-7, we validated the model’s ability to reproduce clinical outcomes in independent cohorts. Simulated CAR T-cell pharmacokinetics were compared to a cohort of 33 individual patients’ trajectories of CAR T-cell abundance following axi-cel treatment, stratified by response status (19). Stratification of the simulated CAR T-cell trajectories resulted in similar distributions of pharmacokinetics for both response statuses (Figure 2A). We performed normalized prediction distribution errors (npde) analysis to investigate the accuracy of simulated pharmacokinetics (20) (Figure S1). The resulting quantile-quantile plot compares the distribution of npde to a normal distribution (Figure 2A, Figure S2A-D). The pop-PD were compared to an independent cohort that measured 47 patients’ tumor burdens at three time-points following axi-cel treatment via circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) (3). Similarly, these patients were stratified by response status, and for each timepoint and response status the observed and simulated ctDNA distributions were statistically indistinguishable (Figure 2B). These results demonstrate that the pop-PK/PD model reproduces outcomes in independent cohorts for metrics it was calibrated on (CAR T-cell pharmacokinetics) and was not calibrated on (kinetics of lymphoma death).

We further assessed the validated model’s ability to capture the impact of tumor burden on the efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy. We first compared tumor size distributions for actual and simulated patients exhibiting either response or progression in ZUMA-1, measured as ctDNA by Frank et al. (21) (Figure 3A). Clinical and simulated results showed significantly higher pre-treatment tumor burden in patients experiencing disease progression compared with patients experiencing durable responses. Further, observed and simulated ctDNA distributions were statistically indistinguishable within each group (Figure 3A). We next stratified PFS distributions according to pre-treatment tumor burden and observed that the pop-PK/PD model reproduces the hazard ratio (HR) for disease progression observed between smaller versus larger tumors (observed HR 0.16 [95% C.I. 0.07–0.37], simulated HR 0.10 [0.04–0.21]) (21) (Figure 3B). Finally, as reported in the ZUMA-1 trial, logistic regression of both actual and simulated trials demonstrated a significant relationship between the ratio of peak number of CAR T-cells to initial tumor size and the probability that a patient will experience a durable response (15) (Figure 3C). Together, these results demonstrate that this pop-PK/PD model reproduces the observed prognostic impact of high tumor burden. The model suggests a quantitative mechanism for this relationship: rapid progression occurs when the ratio of tumor cells to CAR T-cells is sufficiently high that tumor cell killing by CAR T-cells is outpaced by the rate of new tumor cell production by cell division. In this scenario, individual CAR T-cells are almost constantly engaged in lymphoma cell killing resulting in chronic antigen stimulation (Figure 3D). Although T-cell exhaustion was not an explicit cell state in the pharmacokinetic model, this simulation output is consistent with the clinical observation that chronic stimulation results in treatment failure, occurring most often in large lymphomas (22). Finally, the simulation illustrates that temporary remissions occur when tumor cell killing outpaces tumor proliferation, but the duration of high CAR T-cell abundance is too brief to drive the tumor cell population to extinction.

We next explored the impact of treatments that shrink tumors prior to CAR T-cell infusion, referred to as bridging therapies. The pop-PK/PD model predicted that for each 2-fold reduction in tumor burden, an additional 10% of patients will remain progression-free at 12 months (Figure 4A). A recent retrospective analysis by Roddie et al. on the effect of bridging therapy response on CAR T-cell efficacy also observed that patients with a complete (CR) or partial response (PR) to bridging therapy had significantly less risk of progression than patients who did not respond to bridging therapy (progressive (PD) or stable disease (SD)) (5) (Figure 4B). Although patients who needed bridging appear to be a higher risk than the population enrolled in ZUMA-7, the observed benefit of responding to bridging therapy was close to the predicted effect of 88% reduction in tumor population. This magnitude of tumor debulking is consistent with the observed efficacy of common systemic bridging therapies, epcoritamab, or a combination of polatuzumab-vedotin, bendamustine, and rituximab, which elicit average lesion size reductions of 81% (23) and 87% (24), respectively, among responders. Similarly, bridging radiotherapy has been observed to reduce metabolic tumor volume by a median of 72% among the majority of patients who experience cytoreduction (6), and in a real-world study, bridging radiotherapy independently associated with improved PFS in a multivariate analysis (25). Attainable magnitudes of tumor debulking from bridging therapy demonstrate a benefit in CAR T therapeutic outcomes.

We explored other models of debulking therapy response. First, since not all patients will respond to bridging therapy, we simulated the effect of bridging therapy when 50% of patients respond, consistent with clinical experience (5,6). This simulation, which reflects a trial of axi-cel with or without debulking therapy, predicted a 35% reduction in risk of disease progression (Figure 4C). We also investigated whether the predicted benefit of bridging was apparent in two other CAR T-cell products approved to treat LBCL, tisa-cel and liso-cel. Recalibration of the model to the pharmacokinetic and PFS outcomes of these CAR T products from the JULIET (tisa-cel) (26) or TRANSCEND (liso-cel) (27) trials predicted a benefit of bridging for both products, with larger benefit in tisa-cel consistent with clinical observations by Roddie et al (5) (Figure S3A-B). Furthermore, adjustments in model parameters alter, but do not negate, the benefit of bridging therapy (Figure S4). Another potential benefit of debulking therapy is that a smaller lymphoma population logically has a smaller chance that one or more cells will acquire resistance to CD19 CAR T-cells by CD19 loss (28). We adapted the pop-PK/PD model to include a stochastic probability of CD19 loss, calibrated to reproduce the observed incidence of CD19-negative relapse in a trial of axi-cel (28). Killing 88% of lymphoma cells by bridging therapy is predicted by this model to halve the incidence of CD19-negative relapse and improve PFS following CAR T-cell therapy (Figure S5A-C).

Changing the timing of treatment could provide an alternative means of exploiting the superior efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy against smaller tumors, without a need for bridging therapy. Axi-cel is currently approved for second-line treatment of primary refractory LBCL or LBCL that relapses within one year of initial therapy. Waiting for relapse in high-risk patients allows lymphoma to grow larger, which is associated with a higher risk of failure of CAR T-cell therapy (3). Although most LBCL patients are cured by first-line chemoimmunotherapy, high-sensitivity liquid biopsies make it possible to accurately identify which patients are likely to relapse (17,29,30). Therefore, high-risk patients with detectable ctDNA at the end of first-line treatment might benefit from earlier CAR T-cell therapy. We simulated CAR T-cell therapy in this scenario using a virtual cohort of high-risk lymphoma patients (International Prognostic Index (IPI) ≥ 3) with tumor burdens based on clinically measured distributions of ctDNA levels in patients with detectable ctDNA at the end of first-line therapy (EOT; n=18 patients) or at the time of CAR T-cell infusion after disease progression following first-line therapy (n=86 patients) (Figure 4D). ctDNA quantities were on average 100-fold lower at end of therapy than at the time of disease progression (1.5 (0.4 – 20) hGE/mL at EOT versus 44 (6 – 626) hGE/mL at infusion), indicating lower tumor burden and the potential for greater efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy. Simulations of CAR T therapy upon disease progression (as is standard), or immediately after first-line therapy for patients who are ctDNA-positive at end of therapy, predict that ctDNA-guided CAR T cell therapy would approximately halve the risk of second disease progression (PFS2, calculated since initiating first-line therapy to avoid lead-time bias) compared to the standard practice of waiting for disease progression (HR: 0.43 (0.34, 0.55)), (Figure 4E).

## Discussion

Efforts to improve the efficacy of CAR T-cells are warranted both because of their high costs (>$500,000 per patient (31)) and because their curative potential is presently realized in only half of patients (2). This pre-clinical study, which simulated clinical trials, identified tumor debulking before CAR T-cell infusion as a critical point of intervention that could improve the rate of success of existing CAR T-cell products. We simulated two strategies, (1) tumor debulking before CAR T-cell infusion and (2) deploying CAR T-cell therapy against measurable residual disease (MRD) at the end of first-line treatment, rather than waiting for frank relapse. Regarding tumor debulking, our model provides a mechanistic rationale for the observation that patients whose tumor burden is reduced by bridging radiotherapy experience survival comparable to those with initially low burden (5,6,25,32), supporting the hypothesis that tumor debulking improves the efficacy of CAR T-cell therapies. While bridging is used to control disease that poses an immediate clinical risk, our model suggests an additional rationale: reducing disease burden whenever it is likely to undermine CAR T efficacy. Patients with greater disease burden are likely to benefit most and may be identified by a number of features including metabolic tumor volume, ctDNA, or elevated serum LDH (3). Regarding MRD-guided therapy, Roschewski et al has explained that detection of MRD in lymphoma enables initiation of salvage therapies before clinical relapse and that the efficacy of early intervention is an important question that requires study in clinical trials (30). The presented models can assist in the design of such trials and predict that different strategies in the use of existing CAR T-cell products may reduce the risk of disease progression by 35 to 55%, suggesting that future studies to optimize bridging therapy or MRD-guided therapy have the potential to improve survival in relapsed or refractory LBCL.

Use of CAR T-cells in the first-line of treatment for high-risk LBCL is already being studied in phase 2 and 3 trials. The phase 2 ZUMA-12 study reported a 78% complete response rate with axi-cel therapy after two-cycles of RCHOP for patients with high-risk LBCL (defined as either double- or triple-hit lymphoma or LBCL with IPI ≥ 3) (33), and the phase 3 study of this strategy is presently recruiting (ZUMA-23, NCT05605899) (34). The phase 2 ALPHA3 trial uses liquid biopsy at the end of first-line chemoimmunotherapy to select MRD-positive patients for consolidation by allogeneic CAR T-cell therapy (35). Thus, our modelled scenario of liquid-biopsy guided consolidation for high-risk LBCL mirrors current clinical trials, supporting its feasibility. A critical question of such strategies is how they will affect the cost of lymphoma treatment. Approximately half of patients with IPI ≥ 3 LBCL (36) and 30% of double-hit lymphoma patients (37) remain progression-free for at least five years after standard first-line chemoimmunotherapy, and therefore do not need CAR T-cell therapy at first-line. If the ZUMA-23 study is positive, the number of LCBL patients indicated for CAR T-cells could dramatically increase. Conversely, patient selection by MRD would limit the use of CAR T-cells to patients who were not cured by standard chemoimmunotherapy. Therefore, patient selection by liquid biopsy may be a cost-saving intervention. Furthermore, if the deployment of CAR T-cells against smaller, more easily treatable tumors leads to higher rates of durable remission, then the greater gain in survival would improve the cost efficiency of CAR T-cells (31). Therefore, the strategies studied are of growing health and economic importance as CAR T-cell therapies are increasingly evaluated at the first-line of treatment (33,34).

The established prognostic value of CAR T:tumor ratio is consistent with worse outcomes observed in concurrent nodal and extranodal disease, because this generally entails higher tumor burden (15,38). Iacobini et al also identified evidence of site-specific resistance, particularly reduced clearance of liver, adrenal, and pancreatic lesions (38); PK/PD principles suggest this may result from lower CAR T exposure or killing rates at those sites. This motivates a pragmatic use of bridging: ‘debulking’ hard-to-control extranodal sites, even if not conventionally ‘bulky’, could improve local CAR T:tumor ratios and the chance of disease control. Our present model addresses total burden, but PK/PD models can extend to multi-compartment disease.

We analyzed LBCL, but the principle that smaller populations of cancer cells are more easily eradicated could apply to other malignancies treated by CAR T-cells. Notably, a response to bridging therapy has been observed to improve the efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) as it does in LBCL (39). A important caveat learned from studies in ALL is that high-intensity bridging that delays CAR T-cell infusion and/or elicits high-grade toxicities does not improve survival compared to shorter and tolerable low-intensity bridging (39). The approach of our study could be adapted to other hematological cancers by similarly building pharmacodynamic models atop existing population-pharmacokinetic models of approved CAR T-cell therapies for ALL, multiple myeloma, and follicular lymphoma (40).

This pharmacological modeling study has limitations and does not justify changes to current clinical practice. Instead, like other preclinical studies of treatment strategies, it suggests therapeutic hypotheses that warrant clinical study. The hypothesis that debulking tumors with bridging therapy can improve CAR T-cell efficacy is supported by retrospective analyses of patients who received bridging therapy (5,6,25,32), but the potential benefit of administering bridging therapy to less restricted set of eligible patients before CAR T-cell infusion is best suited to prospective study. By design, our pop-PK/PD model has sufficient complexity to investigate the prognostic impact of tumor size and its reduction, but omits many biological aspects of CAR T-cells and lymphoma. We analyzed plausible simplified scenarios, such as 50% of patients experiencing ~85% reduction in tumor burden. However, real responses are variable, and our approach is conservative because some patients experience stronger responses to bridging. The concern that treatment of disease with fewer CD19 expressing tumor cells might reduce CAR T-cell expansion has been dispelled by recent findings that axi-cel expansion is equal or improved in patients with complete responses to bridging therapy (41). Lastly, we have not investigated specific bridging modalities, which should be well tolerated and pose no barrier to subsequent CAR T-cell therapy. A bridging therapy whose adverse effects hinder CAR T-cell therapy administration would likely worsen outcomes. In this regard, several retrospective series indicate that bridging radiotherapy elicits high rates of local control and associates with improved outcomes (4,6,25,42). Ultimately, our study pinpoints bridging therapy as an intervention whose benefits could be more impactful than ‘buying time’. If holding or bridging therapy is to be employed more often, selecting approaches that maximize safety and debulking efficacy is a vital question for empiric clinical study.

## Methods

### Population pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model

The population-pharmacokinetic element of the model was developed by Stein et. al and applied to tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) (16). It is a piecewise function that includes an initial CAR T-cell expansion phase and then a decline phase for two populations of CAR T-cells, effector T-cells and memory T-cells (Figure 1A). The model has six parameters: the maximum number of CAR T-cells ( c m a x ), the fold expansion of CAR T-cells ( f o l d x ), the fraction of CAR T-cells that are memory T-cells ( F B ), the time at which the CAR T-cell population is at its maximum size ( T m a x ), and the decline rates for effector T-cells and memory T-cells ( α and β ). In this mixed-effects model, each parameter has a population mean (fixed effect) and standard deviation (random effects), resulting in inter-individual variation. Fixed and random effect parameters were calibrated by Stein et al. to reproduce clinically observed kinetics of tisa-cel (16). We adjusted these parameters to fit clinically observed kinetics for axi-cel (18) (Table S1). The equation describing the pharmacokinetics of the total number of CAR T-cells is as follows: T t o t a l t = R 0 e ρ t , t < T m a x A e - α t - T m a x + B e - β t - T m a x , t ≥ T m a x where R 0 = c m a x / f o l d x , A = c m a x 1 - F B , B = c m a x F B , and ρ = ln ( f o l d x ) / T m a x .

The pharmacodynamic element of the model follows a well-established framework that has been employed in prior models of CAR T-cell therapy: cancer cells grow, and can be bound and killed by CAR T-cells (8–14). The model therefore includes 3 species: lymphoma cells ( L ), free CAR T-cells ( T ), and CAR T-cells bound to lymphoma cells ( C ) (Figure 1A). The population of free CAR T-cells is set so that the sum of T and C equals T t o t a l from the pharmacokinetic model. The system of ordinary differential equations governing the pharmacodynamics is as follows: d L d t = g L - k L T d T d t = - k L T + ω C + r T t o t a l - T + C d C d t = k L T - ω C where g is the growth rate of lymphoma cells, k is the rate at which lymphoma and CAR T-cells associate, ω is the rate at which CAR T-cells kill lymphoma cells when in complex, and r is a conversion factor from transgenes/μg genomic DNA (the units used for T t o t a l in the PK model) to number of lymphoma cells in a person. The initial number of lymphoma cells ( L 0 ) was sampled from a clinically observed distribution of initial LBCL burden (17), the initial number of CAR T-cells ( T 0 ) was T t o t a l ( t = 0 ) from the pharmacokinetic model, and the initial number of CAR T-cell/lymphoma complexes ( C 0 ) was zero. Pharmacodynamic parameter values are in Table S2.

### Simulation of progression free survival

Progression free survival (PFS) was simulated by calculating the time at which each simulated patient experiences a progression event, which was defined as lymphoma population surpassing four times its original size. Simulated patients are considered cured if their number of tumor cells is less than one, and if they had no progression event within two-years, they were marked as censored at two years. PFS distributions were simulated the same way for all tested scenarios.

To compare CAR T-cell therapy as second-line treatment for relapsed disease versus its use as consolidation for Measure Residual Disease, we simulated distributions of time to second disease progression (PFS2) following first-line chemoimmunotherapy. The distribution of PFS2 for patients who experience first progression within one year of receiving RCHOP was generated by sampling the time of relapse from the clinically observed RCHOP distribution for high-risk (IPI≥3) LBCL patients (36) and adding the additional time that patients would not experience a progression event after CAR T-cell therapy. In the standard scenario of treatment at relapse, patients who were relapsed or refractory to first-line therapy received CAR T-cell therapy directly after first progression. In the alternative scenario of MRD-guided treatment, patients who were refractory to first-line therapy received CAR T-cell therapy directly after their progression event while patients who were MRD-positive at the end of chemoimmunotherapy received CAR T-cells directly after RCHOP.

### Parameter estimation

The pop-PK model parameters were adjusted from published values for tisa-cel to align with the observed pharmacokinetics of axi-cel. The manually adjusted parameters were the maximum number of CAR T-cells ( c m a x ), the fold change in CAR T-cell abundance during the expansion phase ( f o l d x ), and the decay rates of the effector and memory T-cell populations ( α and β ) (Table S1). Two of the PD parameters were fit so that simulated PFS distribution matched the observed distribution in the ZUMA-7 trial: the rate at which lymphoma and CAR T-cells associate ( k ) and the rate at which CAR T-cells kill lymphoma cells ( ω ). Since the biophysical affinity of the anti-CD19 single-chain variable fragment to CD19 is not expected to differ among patients, k was constant. Conversely, ω was allowed to vary across patients, reflecting inter-patient variability in CAR T-cell quality. The third parameter, growth rate ( g ) was set by published doubling times of aggressive Non-Hodgkin Lymphomas in human patients, based on serial tumor volume measurements (43). We performed sensitivity analysis of the fitted PK and PD analysis to confirm that the parameters minimized error between clinical and simulated outcomes for both pharmacokinetics and PFS (Figure S1).

### Normalized prediction distribution errors (npde) analysis

The pop-PK model was validated by performing normalized prediction distribution errors (npde) analysis using the npde library in R (20). The npde analysis compared the simulated pharmacokinetics to the observed pharmacokinetics of 33 individuals in an independent validation data set (19) (Figure S2A-D).

### Clinical ctDNA distributions

Simulated treatment outcomes for virtual cohorts of patients with distributions of initial tumor burden matched either the clinically observed tumor burdens after first-line RCHOP treatment or prior to CAR T-cell infusion. This clinical observations came from recent ctDNA studies that obtained plasma samples at the end of therapy from previously untreated LBCL patients undergoing curative intent therapy (29), and on the day of CAR T-cell infusion from relapsed/refractory LBCL patients receiving standard of care axi-cel (3). These studies profiled single-nucleotide variants and phased variants, defined as multiple mutations on a single DNA molecule, as previously described (44). ctDNA levels were measured in haploid genome equivalents per milliliter (hGE/mL), calculated as the product of total cell-free DNA concentration and the mean allele-fraction of somatic mutations or phased variants. Primary sequencing data from patients undergoing CAR T-cell therapy have previously been deposited in dbGaP (phs003145.v1.p1). Primary sequencing data from the remaining patients cannot be uploaded because of consent restrictions.
